Empathy, congruence, UPR.q: A therapist tries to see the situation from the client's point of view. Which part of person-centered therapy is this?
wrong: Congruence, being genuine and open with the client at all times

Active listening.q: A therapist says, "So what I'm hearing is that you feel ignored at home. Is that right?" What technique is this?
wrong: Free association, saying whatever comes to mind
That is the patient speaking freely.

Active listening.right: "So you feel left out. Is that right?"
wrong: "That belief is irrational, and here is why you should drop it."

Active listening.q: Active listening is a central part of which therapy?
wrong: Ellis's rational emotive behavior therapy for irrational beliefs
Active listening.exp: Active listening is central to Rogers' client-centered therapy.

Cognitive therapy.q: A therapist teaches a client that his thoughts about events, not the events themselves, drive his feelings. Which therapy is this?
wrong: Psychodynamic therapy exploring the unconscious mind
Cognitive therapy.exp: Thoughts come between events and emotions.

Cognitive therapy.q: What is the core idea of cognitive therapy?
Cognitive therapy.right: Thoughts come between events and emotions
wrong: Emotions come only from hidden childhood memories we can't reach
Cognitive therapy.exp: Cognitive therapy: change thoughts to change emotional reactions.

Cognitive therapy.q: Which two methods does cognitive therapy use, according to your slides?
wrong: Free association and dream interpretation in long weekly sessions
Cognitive therapy.exp: Methods: cognitive restructuring and fear hierarchies.

Cognitive restructuring.q: A therapist helps a client replace "I'll never make it" with "I can improve if I keep practicing." Which method is this?
wrong: Systematic desensitization with a fear hierarchy

Cognitive restructuring.q: A student thinks, "I bombed one test, so I'll fail out of school." Which response is cognitive restructuring?
Cognitive restructuring.right: "One test doesn't decide my grade; I can improve."
wrong: "Let's look at what your dreams about school might mean to you."
"You'll earn a sticker for each study hour."
That is part of systematic desensitization.
Cognitive restructuring.exp: Challenge the pessimistic thought and replace it with a positive one.

Cognitive restructuring.q: Which pair shows the two steps of cognitive restructuring?
Cognitive restructuring.right: Challenge a thought, then replace it
wrong: Relax first, and then face each feared situation one step at a time
Cognitive restructuring.exp: Recognize and challenge pessimistic thoughts, then replace them.

Socratic questioning.q: A therapist asks, "What evidence do you have that everyone hates you?" Which strategy is this?
wrong: Active listening, restating what the client said

Socratic questioning.q: A therapist asks, "How might your best friend see this situation differently?" Which strategy is this?
wrong: Unconditional positive regard toward the client's every feeling
That is acceptance, not challenging thoughts.
That is saying whatever comes to mind.
Socratic questioning.exp: Deep questions that challenge your thoughts.

Socratic questioning.q: Socratic questioning is a strategy within which method?
wrong: Systematic desensitization with relaxation and a fear hierarchy

Fear hierarchy.q: A therapist and client list feared situations from "seeing a photo of a dog" up to "petting a dog." What did they make?
wrong: A token economy chart of rewards for good behavior
Fear hierarchy.exp: Feared situations ranked from least to most anxiety-provoking.

Fear hierarchy.q: A client afraid of dogs ranks situations from "seeing a dog picture" up to "petting a dog." How is this list used?
Fear hierarchy.right: To face fears gradually, least to most
wrong: To decide which dog-related dreams to interpret in the next session
Fear hierarchy.exp: Fear hierarchies let people face fears gradually in a safe way.

Fear hierarchy.q: Which therapy builds a fear hierarchy and adds relaxation techniques?
wrong: Aversion therapy, which pairs an unwanted behavior with discomfort
Fear hierarchy.exp: Systematic desensitization: fear hierarchy plus relaxation.

Beck's cognitive theory of depression.q: Which theory says depressed people develop negative ways of thinking about themselves, the world and the future?
wrong: The dopamine hypothesis about chemical imbalance
Beck's cognitive theory of depression.exp: Aaron Beck: faulty information processing and the negative triad.

Beck's cognitive theory of depression.q: According to Aaron Beck, what makes people vulnerable to depression?
wrong: Low dopamine levels in the brain's reward pathway and nothing else
Beck's cognitive theory of depression.exp: Faulty information processing and core irrational beliefs.

Beck's cognitive theory of depression.q: Which pattern do depressed people develop, according to Beck?
wrong: A fear hierarchy ranked from least to most anxiety-provoking
That is used in exposure therapy.
That is the bond with a therapist.
Beck's cognitive theory of depression.exp: Negative thoughts about self, world and future.

Negative cognitive triad.q: A depressed teen thinks, "I'm worthless, nobody cares about me, and it will never get better." What does this show?
wrong: A delusion of persecution that others are out to get him
These are negative thoughts, not paranoid beliefs.

Negative cognitive triad.q: "Things will never get better" is a negative thought about which part of the triad?
wrong: Yourself, as in thinking you are worthless or a failure
That would be "No one cares about me."
The triad is self, world, future.

Negative cognitive triad.q: "No one cares about me" is a negative thought about which part of the triad?
wrong: The future, as in thinking nothing will ever improve
That would be "Things will never get better."
The triad is self, world, future.

Behavioral therapies.q: Which therapies apply conditioning principles, like exposure, aversion and token economies?
wrong: Humanistic therapies built on acceptance and empathy

Behavioral therapies.q: Which list contains only behavioral therapies?
wrong: Free association, dream interpretation, hypnosis and active listening

Behavioral therapies.q: What principle do all behavioral therapies apply?
wrong: Uncovering the unconscious through dreams and free association

Exposure therapy.q: A therapist has a client who fears elevators ride one, again and again, until the fear fades. Which therapy is this?
wrong: Aversion therapy, pairing a behavior with discomfort
Exposure therapy.exp: Facing what you would normally avoid.

Exposure therapy.q: Your slide links exposure therapy to which classic example?
wrong: Phineas Gage and the iron rod through his prefrontal cortex

Exposure therapy.q: A client who fears crowds is helped to spend more and more time in busy places until the fear fades. Which therapy is this?
wrong: Aversion therapy, making the feared thing feel even more unpleasant
Aversion makes an unwanted behavior unpleasant.
Exposure therapy.exp: Exposing people to what they would normally avoid.

Systematic desensitization.q: A client learns relaxation techniques, then works up a fear hierarchy step by step while staying relaxed. Which therapy is this?
wrong: Aversion therapy, the opposite kind of conditioning
Aversion makes things unpleasant; this makes fears calm.

Systematic desensitization.q: Which two ingredients define systematic desensitization?
wrong: Antabuse and a pleasant behavior that the client wants to stop doing
Systematic desensitization.exp: Least scary to most scary, while staying relaxed.

Systematic desensitization.q: Why is aversion therapy called the opposite of systematic desensitization?
Systematic desensitization.right: One adds discomfort; the other removes fear
wrong: One uses medication while the other uses only talk therapy sessions
Systematic desensitization.exp: Desensitization pairs fears with calm; aversion pairs a behavior with discomfort.

Aversion therapy.q: A man trying to quit nail-biting paints his nails with a bitter-tasting polish. Which therapy does this match?
wrong: That reduces fear; this makes a habit unpleasant.
Aversion therapy.exp: Pairing an unpleasant state with an unwanted behavior.

Aversion therapy.q: A smoker gets a mild unpleasant shock each time he reaches for a cigarette. Which therapy does this match?
wrong: Systematic desensitization through relaxation and a fear hierarchy
That reduces fear, not unwanted behavior.
ECT causes a seizure to treat depression.
Aversion therapy.exp: Pairing an unpleasant state with an unwanted behavior.

Aversion therapy.q: What kind of conditioning is aversion therapy?
wrong: Operant conditioning with rewards like tokens and privileges
That is control of body responses.
Aversion therapy.exp: Aversion therapy is a type of counterconditioning.

Antabuse.q: A patient takes a drug that makes him feel sick if he drinks alcohol. What is it, and what therapy does it represent?
wrong: Lithium, a mood stabilizer used for bipolar disorder
Antabuse.exp: Antabuse pairs drinking with feeling sick.

Antabuse.q: Why does Antabuse help some people stop drinking?
Antabuse.right: Drinking now makes them feel sick
wrong: It blocks dopamine so that alcohol no longer feels rewarding at all
Not how it's described on your slides.
Antabuse.exp: Pairs a negative outcome with a previously pleasant stimulus.

Antabuse.q: Antabuse is the most common example of which therapy?
wrong: Systematic desensitization for phobias and other intense fears

Token economy.q: In a hospital unit, patients earn points for making their beds and trade them for privileges. What procedure is this?
wrong: Aversion therapy that makes the behavior unpleasant
Token economy.exp: Operant conditioning with tokens for desired behavior.

Token economy.q: A child earns a gold star for each completed chore and trades five for a toy. Which procedure is this?
wrong: Aversion therapy that makes skipping chores very unpleasant

Token economy.q: A token economy is based on which kind of conditioning?
wrong: Counterconditioning, like the aversion therapy of Antabuse
Not a type on your slides.

Biofeedback.q: Sensors show a patient her heart rate on a screen so she can learn to slow it on purpose. What technique is this?
wrong: rTMS, which uses magnetic pulses on the brain
That induces relaxation, not feedback from sensors.
Biofeedback.exp: Learning to consciously control physiological responses.

Biofeedback.q: Which part of biofeedback lets the person learn to control a body response?
wrong: Taking a medication that slows the heart down automatically
Biofeedback.exp: Sensors feed data back; with practice they learn to influence it.

Biofeedback.q: Which response could a person learn to control through biofeedback?
wrong: Their genetic predisposition to developing a disorder later on
Genes can't be controlled this way.
Biofeedback.exp: Physiological responses like heart rate and muscle tension.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).q: A therapist helps a client change both her negative thoughts and her avoidance behaviors. Which therapy is this?
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).exp: CBT applies both cognitive and behavioral principles.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).q: A therapist helps a client notice anxious thoughts and also practice going to parties step by step. Which therapy combines these?
wrong: Psychoanalysis, exploring unconscious childhood conflicts and dreams
That doesn't target thoughts and behaviors directly.
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).exp: CBT applies both cognitive and behavioral principles.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).q: What is the core idea behind CBT?
wrong: Behavior comes only from rewards and has nothing to do with thinking
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).exp: People's thinking influences their emotions and behavior.

Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT).q: A modified form of CBT helps a client with borderline personality disorder manage intense emotions. Which therapy is this?
wrong: REBT, which confronts irrational beliefs head-on
Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT).exp: DBT was originally developed for borderline personality disorder.

Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT).q: DBT is a modified form of which therapy?
wrong: Psychoanalysis, the therapy of free association and dreams
Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT).exp: DBT is a modified form of CBT.

wrong: Uncover unconscious conflicts through dreams and free association
Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT).exp: Manage intense emotions, improve relationships, build a life worth living.

The 4 DBT skills.q: Which list shows the four DBT skills?
The 4 DBT skills.right: Mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness
wrong: Empathy, congruence, unconditional positive regard, active listening, free association
The 4 DBT skills.exp: Mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness.

The 4 DBT skills.q: During a crisis, a client gets through without making things worse. Which DBT skill is she using?
wrong: Interpersonal effectiveness, keeping relationships while getting needs met
That is understanding and changing emotions.
The 4 DBT skills.exp: Distress tolerance: managing a crisis without making it worse.

The 4 DBT skills.q: A client asks a friend for help while keeping the friendship strong. Which DBT skill is this?
wrong: Distress tolerance, getting through a crisis without making it worse
The 4 DBT skills.exp: Getting needs met and keeping relationships.

Rational emotive behavior therapy (REBT).q: A therapist bluntly challenges a client's belief that he must be perfect, saying it's irrational. Which therapy is this?
wrong: Person-centered therapy, which accepts without judging

Rational emotive behavior therapy (REBT).q: What are the three steps of REBT?
wrong: Relax, rank fears from least to most, and then face each one in turn
Rational emotive behavior therapy (REBT).exp: Identify, challenge and replace irrational beliefs.

Rational emotive behavior therapy (REBT).q: REBT is mainly used for which problem?
wrong: Schizophrenia's positive symptoms like hallucinations and delusions

Modes of therapy.q: Individual and group therapy describe what, rather than the type of therapy?
wrong: Which disorders the therapy is able to treat and cure

Modes of therapy.q: A client asks whether she'll get CBT or person-centered therapy. Is that a question about the "mode" of therapy?
Modes of therapy.right: No; mode is individual or group
wrong: Yes; mode means the type of therapy, like CBT or psychoanalysis
Mode is how therapy is delivered.
Modes of therapy.exp: Modes: how therapy is delivered (individual or group), not the type.

Modes of therapy.q: Which choice is about the mode of therapy?
wrong: CBT vs. REBT, two different cognitive behavioral approaches
That is the type of therapy.

Group therapy.q: Five people who have lost a loved one meet weekly with a therapist and realize they aren't alone. Which mode is this?
wrong: Individual therapy, one-on-one with a therapist
That is a type, not a mode.
Group therapy.exp: Cheaper, reduces isolation, shows you aren't the only one.

Group therapy.q: A teen with social anxiety joins a group of peers with the same problem. Which benefit of group therapy does this give him?
Group therapy.right: He sees he isn't the only one
wrong: He gets fully personalized one-on-one attention every week
Group therapy.exp: Group therapy shows people they aren't alone, is cheaper, and relieves isolation.

Group therapy.q: Why might a clinic recommend group therapy to a client on a tight budget?
wrong: It is more personalized than any other kind of therapy

Individual therapy.q: A client needs a personalized, private approach and flexible scheduling, and can afford it. Which mode fits best?
wrong: Group therapy, which is cheaper and less private
It is less personalized and private.

Individual therapy.q: Which is a drawback of individual therapy on your slides?
wrong: It is less personalized than group therapy for most clients
Individual therapy.exp: Personalized, intimate and flexible, but very expensive.

Individual therapy.q: Why might a therapist choose individual over group therapy for a client?
Individual therapy.right: Some disorders don't treat well in groups
wrong: Group therapy is always more expensive than individual therapy
Individual therapy.exp: Some disorders can't be treated well in a group.
